blocks.x: Mosi-ao-Tunya—or the smoke that thunders—is the local name for Zimbabwe's Victoria Falls: a nod to the sound and fury of the cascades that straddle Zambia and Zimbabwe. From half a mile away, on the Zimbabwe side, the spray cools on my face. It's a welcome refreshment on a warm autumn morning.
Closer still to the falls, the mist is heavy enough to drench the sightseers stopping to gawk at the spectacle from viewing points, or on slippery pathways between the various lookouts.

The 1,700-meter-wide falls are undeniably impressive—after all, this is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and considered one of the seven natural wonders of the world. But I'm even more taken by the fact that its white spray often obscures the view entirely, leaving just the incessant and all-encompassing roar of the water in the air.

The nearby town of Victoria Falls is far noisier and busier than I'd imagined. “It used to be a small town, but now it has been reclassified as a city,” says Savanah Du Preez, the camp manager at newly opened Mpala Jena Private Villas. Having grown up in and around Victoria Falls, she remembers coming across baboons and wild buffalo on the roads while walking to and from school, she tells me. “Now there are craft beer pubs and gourmet restaurants.”
https://media.cntraveler.com/photos/6ac7b6d8d2ece3ae899e3e56/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/2021-GP-Wildlife-Zimbabwe-MpalaJenaCamp-012.jpg

blocks.x: ‎Elephants can be seen in the bushes, and crossing the mighty Zambezi River, in Zambezi National Park.
Andrew Howard Photo/ Courtesy Mpala Jena Camp

The heart of this town is a neat grid of small roads, lined with shops selling tours and safari trips amid a jumble of souvenirs and handicrafts, alongside a smattering of local eateries. I didn't expect to get wood-fired pizzas and chicken masala pies in Victoria Falls, but a clutch of little bakeries and cafes have sprung up to service the ever-growing tourism to the area.

But while tourism has boomed, the area still belongs to the wildlife. The town is encircled by protected Zambezi National Park, where animals roam freely throughout its 56,000 hectares. One morning, as we take a pitstop near a 1,200-year-old giant baobab known as the “Big Tree”, my guide Gerald Sibanda points out a huge elephant lurking in the bushes, with tusks like spears. “We still see leopards while driving in the night,” he says.

While leopards remain characteristically elusive during my stay, Zambezi National Park rewards in other ways. The boat transfer from Kalambezi jetty, at one end of Victoria Falls town, to my Mpala Jena villa is itself a safari of sorts. Barely 10 minutes into the journey, we spot two elephants swimming across the river, their trunks popping up into the air every few minutes. “They are coming from Zambia to Zimbabwe—they have no need for passports,” Gerald laughs. Matching my best safari sightings over the years, the sight of a mother helping her calf deftly navigate the mighty Zambezi and clamber up the muddy banks moves me to tears.

Great Plains Conservation

Located just a few minutes upstream from the Mpala Jena luxury safari camp on the banks of the Zambezi River, my three-bedroom villa, one of two to open in late 2025, is designed to blend airy Italian design straight from Puglia—think drystone walls and conical roofs—with earthy African decor, from rattan accents and earthy terracottas to thatching.

The villa is spread out on a private island, with a central living and dining space, and three spacious suites on either side. Each of the suites comes with its own al-fresco bathing area and a verandah for hot afternoons, from where you can watch the local wildlife without leaving the room. My favorite spot quickly becomes a loungey beanbag by the swimming pool—conveniently located next to the pool bar with a direct view of the great river.
https://media.cntraveler.com/photos/6ac7b6d8d2ece3ae899e3e58/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/2025-GreatPlains_Mpala-Jena-Villa-IA-121.jpg
